title: 論語 子罕第九
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 9, 〈子罕〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 9 of the Analects, 子罕 Zǐ hǎn, named, as every book is, from its first words ("The Master seldom…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Much of this book is about the Master himself as others saw him and as he saw himself: the four things he was wholly free of (9.4); his calm when surrounded and threatened at Kuang, sure that Heaven had not meant the heritage of King Wen to perish with him (9.5); his answer to those who wondered at his many skills — he had been poor and humble when young (9.6); his rebuke of Zilu for dressing up disciples as the household officers of a great man he no longer was (9.11); and his musings on selling a fine jade (9.12) and on going to live among the eastern tribes (9.13). Yan Yuan sighs that the Master's Way rises higher the more he looks up at it (9.10). There are many short sayings much quoted since: the river flowing on day and night (9.16), never having met anyone who loved virtue as he loved beauty (9.17), the young who are to be feared, since no one can know they will not match the present (9.22), the common man whose will cannot be taken from him (9.25), the pine and cypress that are last to wither when the year turns cold (9.27), and the wise, the humane and the brave (9.28). Each numbered passage (9.1–9.30, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 9.5 and 9.11 the edition we follow misprints 子 for 予 'I, me'; the reading text is corrected and the notes say so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t: 子罕言利與命與仁。
sentences.l: The Master seldom spoke of profit, and the decree, and humaneness.
sentences.i: Profit, what Heaven ordains, and humaneness: these the Master seldom talked about.
sentences.n: The book is named 子罕 from its first words; Zhu Xi's heading counts thirty chapters (凡三十章); He Yan's counts thirty-one, and adds that Huang Kan's text has thirty. 罕 hǎn 'seldom' (Zhu Xi: 罕，少也; He Yan: 希也). 與 yǔ here is 'and', joining the three objects of 言 'to speak of'. 命 is what Heaven decrees — a man's lot and the order of things. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: reckoning profit harms what is right; the principle of the decree is subtle; the Way of humaneness is great — all three are things the Master seldom spoke of. He Yan's commentary (unattributed): 利 is 'the harmony of what is right' (利者義之和也, a phrase from the Changes); 命 is Heaven's decree; 仁 is the fullness of conduct; few could reach these, so he seldom spoke of them. Readers have long been struck that humaneness is in fact discussed on page after page of the book; both our commentaries nonetheless let 罕 govern all three nouns, and so do we.

sentences.t:
達巷黨人曰：「
大哉孔子！
博學而無所成名！」

morph.gloss: Daxiang — the name of a village district
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
A man of the Daxiang village said: “How great is Master Kong!
Broadly learned, and yet nothing by which he has made a name!”
sentences.i: A man from the village of Daxiang said: “What a great man Master Kong is! His learning is so wide, and yet there is no one thing he is known for.”
sentences.n: 達巷 Daxiang is, Zhu Xi says, the name of the 黨 'village group' (He Yan's Zheng Xuan: five hundred households make a 黨); the man's own name, Zhu Xi adds, has not come down. 大哉 'great — how!': the predicate put first in an exclamation. 孔子 'Master Kong' is how outsiders speak of Confucius. 無所成名 'has nothing by which to make a name': 所 turns 成名 into 'that by which (he) makes a name'. Zhu Xi: he admired the breadth of the Master's learning and regretted that he had not made a name in any single art. Zheng Xuan says the same: broad in the Way and the arts, without making a name in any one.

sentences.t:
子聞之，
謂門弟子曰：「
吾何執？
執御乎？
執射乎？
吾執御矣。」

morph.gloss: deference to elders, a younger brother's duty (later written 悌)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master heard of it and said to the disciples of his school:
“What shall I take up?
Take up driving?
Take up archery?
I will take up driving.”
sentences.i: When the Master heard of this, he said to his disciples: “What should I specialise in, then? Charioteering? Archery? I'll make it charioteering.”
sentences.n: 門弟子 'the disciples of his gate', his school (as 8.3). 吾何執 'I — what shall I take up?': a question word object stands before the verb. 執 'to grasp', here, Zhu Xi says, 'to hold to one thing only' (專執): to specialise. 御 yù is driving a chariot, 射 shè archery — two of the six arts (He Yan's Zheng Xuan: he wished to be named for the lowliest of the six arts). 矣 settles it: 'I will take up driving, then.' Zhu Xi: archery and driving are each a single art, and driving, the work of a man's servant, is the lower of the two; the Master is saying, 'You would have me make a name by holding to something? Then I will hold to driving' — he answers praise with modesty. He quotes Yin Tun: the sage's Way is whole and his virtue complete, and he cannot be pointed to by any one strength; the man of Daxiang saw how great Confucius was and how broad his learning, and regretted that he had no single good thing to be known for — he admired the sage without understanding him.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
麻冕，禮也；
今也純，儉；
吾從衆。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “The rites call for a cap of linen; now people use silk, which costs less, and in this I go along with everyone else.”
sentences.n: 麻冕 'a hemp cap': Zhu Xi identifies it as the black cloth cap (緇布冠). 純 chún here is 'silk' (Zhu Xi and He Yan's Kong Anguo: 純，絲也), not its usual 'pure'. 儉 'sparing, economical' — Zhu Xi: 省約. 今也 'now': 也 marks the pause after a time word. Zhu Xi explains the economy: the cloth cap was made of cloth of thirty 'sheng' 升, and a sheng is eighty threads, so the warp has two thousand four hundred threads — so fine and close that it is hard to make, and silk is cheaper. Kong Anguo: silk is easily made, so he follows the economy. The speech runs on past Zhu Xi's comment into the next unit, which is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
拜下，禮也；
今拜乎上，泰也。
雖違衆，
吾從下。
sentences.l:
Bowing below — that is the rites;
nowadays they bow on top — it is arrogant.
Though it goes against the many,
I follow ‘below’.
sentences.i: To bow at the foot of the steps is what the rites require; now people bow only once they are up in the hall, which is presumptuous. Here I keep to the foot of the steps, even if it means going against everyone else.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: when a minister performs a rite with his lord he should bow at the foot of the hall; the lord declines the honour, and only then does the minister go up and complete the bow. 拜乎上 'bow at the top': 乎 is a preposition here, 'at' (= 於). 泰 'grand', here 'overbearing, arrogant' (Zhu Xi: 驕慢也). 雖 'although'. He Yan's Wang Su gives the same account: ministers of the day had grown arrogant and bowed above; to keep the bow below is respect. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng on the pair: where a custom does no harm to what is right, the gentleman may follow it; where it harms what is right, he may not.

sentences.t:
子絶四：
毋意，
毋必，
毋固，
毋我。
sentences.l:
The Master was utterly without four things:
no private notions,
no insisting,
no stubbornness,
no self.
sentences.i: Four things were wholly absent from the Master: he had no notions of his own to push, no insistence that things must go one way, no stubbornness, and no self to put first.
sentences.n: 絶 jué (the edition's form of 絕) 'to cut off': Zhu Xi — to be without something entirely (無之盡者). 毋 is usually 'do not!', but here, Zhu Xi says, it stands for 無 'not having', and the Shiji, which writes 無, is right; he quotes Master Cheng: this 毋 is not a word of prohibition — the sage was without these four, so what need to forbid them? Zhu Xi's glosses: 意 yì is private intent (私意), 必 insisting in advance on a sure outcome (期必), 固 sticking fast (執滯), 我 the private self (私己). They form a cycle: they start in intent, are carried through by insisting, linger in stubbornness and are completed in the self; intent and insisting come before an affair, stubbornness and self after it, and the self breeds new intent in turn, so that desire for things drags one round without end. He quotes Zhang Zai: have even one of the four and one is unlike Heaven and Earth; and Yang Shi: only someone wise enough to know the sage, watching him closely and taking it in silently, could have recorded this. He Yan's commentary reads each as conduct: no 意, because he took the Way as his measure and did not follow his own will; no 必, because he acted when used and withdrew when set aside; no 固, because nothing was simply allowed or ruled out for him; no 我, because he handed on the old without making it himself and did not set himself apart from others.

sentences.t: 子畏於匡。

morph.gloss: was in danger, on his guard

sentences.l: The Master was in danger at Kuang.
sentences.i: The Master was surrounded and threatened at Kuang.
sentences.n: 畏 wèi is usually 'to fear'; Zhu Xi: here it means to be on one's guard (有戒心之謂). 匡 Kuang is a place. Zhu Xi cites the Shiji: Yang Hu had once done violence at Kuang, and the Master looked like Yang Hu, so the men of Kuang surrounded him. He Yan's Bao Xian tells it more fully: Yan Ke, a disciple of the Master, had been with Yang Hu at that time, and later was driving the Master's chariot when they came to Kuang; the people recognised Ke, and the Master looked like Hu, so they surrounded him with weapons.

sentences.t:
曰：「
文王旣沒，
文不在兹乎？」
sentences.l:
He said: “King Wen being gone,
are letters not here?”
sentences.i: He said: “King Wen is long dead — but is not the pattern he left, the heritage of letters, here, with me?”
sentences.n: 文王 King Wen, father of King Wu, founder of Zhou. 旣 jì (the edition's form of 既) 'already'; 沒 mò 'to die'. 兹 zī 'this, here' (Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo: 此也) — Confucius means himself. 文 is 'letters, the literary arts' (our standing rendering), but Zhu Xi widens it here: the Way where it shows itself is called 文 — the rites, music, and the institutions; and he says the Master speaks of 文 rather than 'the Way' out of modesty. Kong Anguo: though King Wen is dead, his 文 is present here — 'here' is his own person. The speech runs on past Zhu Xi's comment into the next unit, which is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
天之將喪斯文也，
後死者不得與於斯文也；
天之未喪斯文也，
匡人其如予何？
sentences.l:
If Heaven were about to destroy this heritage of letters,
one who died later would not have got to share in it;
since Heaven has not yet destroyed this heritage of letters,
the men of Kuang — what then can they do about me?
sentences.i: If Heaven meant this heritage to perish, it would never have let one born after King Wen have a part in it. Since Heaven has not let it perish, how could the men of Kuang touch me?
sentences.n: The print has 子, a misprint for 予, corrected here. 予 yú 'me' is what the sense needs: Zhu Xi's comment paraphrases the clause as 匡人其奈我何 'what can the men of Kuang do to ME?'; both collation witnesses (Ruan's 1816 text and He Yan's text) read 予; and He Yan's Ma Rong says 如予何 is like saying 奈我何. 如 X 何 is the frame 'what (can one) do with X?' (as 7.22 如予何); 其 adds 'then, after all'. 喪 sàng 'to lose, let perish' (Zhu Xi: 喪與並去聲); 與 yù 'to take part in'. 之 between subject and verb makes 天之將喪斯文 a clause, 'Heaven's being about to destroy this 文', here a supposition, 'if'. 後死者 'the one who dies later' is Confucius himself, later than King Wen. Zhu Xi gives the argument in words he credits to 'Mr Ma' (馬氏) — words that in He Yan's commentary stand partly under Kong Anguo's name: King Wen being dead, Confucius calls himself 'the one who dies after'. If Heaven wished to destroy this 文, it would not have let me share in it; I have shared in it, so Heaven does not wish to destroy it; and if Heaven does not, then what can the men of Kuang do to me? — that is, they cannot go against Heaven to harm me. Compare 7.22, where the Master says the same of Huan Tui.

sentences.t:
大宰問於子貢曰：「
夫子聖者與？
何其多能也？」

morph.gloss: great (read tài: Zhu Xi 大音泰)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Grand Steward asked Zigong:
“Is your Master one who is a sage?
How is it he has so many abilities?”
sentences.i: The Grand Steward asked Zigong: “Your Master — is he a sage? How else could he be so able in so many things?”
sentences.n: 大宰 tài zǎi 'Grand Steward' is a title (Zhu Xi: 大音泰, read tài); He Yan's text writes 太宰. Zhu Xi quotes Mr Kong (孔氏, Kong Anguo): an office; whether of Wu or of Song cannot be known. 子貢 Zigong is Duanmu Ci 端木賜 (1.10). 聖者與 'one who is a sage?': 與 yú (平聲) is the final particle of a doubtful question (Zhu Xi: 與者，疑辭). 何其多能也 'how is it he is so many-abled?' Zhu Xi: the Grand Steward probably took having many abilities to be what made a sage. He Yan's Kong Anguo puts the Steward's question differently: he was puzzled that Confucius was able in so many small skills (疑孔子多能於小藝).

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
固天縱之將聖，
又多能也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “Surely Heaven has given him free rein to be all but a sage,
and besides, he has many abilities.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “Heaven has indeed set no bounds to him, and made him very nearly a sage; that he can do so many things comes on top of that.”
sentences.n: 固 'surely, indeed'. 縱 zòng 'to let loose, give free rein' — Zhu Xi: like 肆, it means there is no limit or measure set to him. 將 jiāng here is 'nearly, all but' (Zhu Xi: 殆也) — a modest word, as though Zigong did not dare claim to know. 又 'besides': Zhu Xi — a sage penetrates everything, and many abilities are a by-product (餘事), so Zigong says 'besides' to add them on. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads 將聖 as 'great sage': Heaven has indeed given him the virtue of a great sage, and also made him able in many things.

sentences.t:
子聞之，曰：「
大宰知我乎？
吾少也賤，
故多能鄙事。
君子多乎哉？
不多也。」

morph.gloss: a steward, the chief officer of a noble house
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master heard of it and said: “Does the Grand Steward know me?
When I was young I was of low station,
so I could do many common things.
Does the gentleman have many? He does not have many.”
sentences.i: When the Master heard of it, he said: “How much does the Grand Steward know of me? I was poor and of no account when I was young, and so I learned to turn my hand to a great many humble jobs. Does a gentleman need so many skills? He does not.”
sentences.n: 少 shào 'young' (Zhu Xi marks it 去聲 at 9.9; here too it is 'young', not shǎo 'few'). 吾少也賤 'I, young — lowly': 也 marks the pause after the time phrase. 鄙事 'common, menial affairs'. 君子多乎哉 'the gentleman — many (abilities)?' with 乎哉 a strong rhetorical question, answered at once: 不多也. 大宰知我乎 can be heard as a question ('does he know me?') or an exclamation ('the Grand Steward knows me!' — a wry admission that he was indeed able in many things); He Yan's text reads 大宰知我者乎 'is the Grand Steward one who knows me?'. Zhu Xi: it was because he was young and lowly that he had many abilities, and what he could do were menial things — it was not that sageliness let him penetrate everything; and since many abilities are no way to lead others, he goes on to say the gentleman need not have them. He Yan's Bao Xian: when I was young and poor I always did things myself, so I could do a lowly man's work; the gentleman ought not to be many-abled.

sentences.t:
牢曰：「
子云：『
吾不試，
故藝。』」
sentences.l:
Lao said: “The Master said:
‘I was not employed,
therefore I am skilled in the arts.’”
sentences.i: Lao said: “The Master once told us: ‘It is because I was never given office that I picked up so many skills.’”
sentences.n: 牢 Lao, Zhu Xi says, was a disciple of Confucius, surname Qin 琴, courtesy name Zikai 子開 or, by another account, Zizhang 子張; He Yan's Zheng Xuan calls him 'the disciple Zilao' (子牢). The text names him by his personal name, and we keep 'Lao'. 云 'to say', introducing a quoted saying. 試 shì 'to try out', here 'to be employed' (Zhu Xi and Zheng Xuan: 試，用也). 藝 yì 'skill, the arts', here used as a verb, 'became skilled'. Zhu Xi: because he was not used by the world, he was able to practise the arts and master them. He quotes Wu (吳氏): when the disciples recorded the Master's words above, Zilao recalled something he had heard before that was close in meaning, and so it was recorded with them — which is why it stands in this chapter.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾有知乎哉？
無知也。
有鄙夫問於我，
空空如也，
我叩其兩端而竭焉。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Do I have knowledge?
I have no knowledge.
There was a common fellow who asked of me,
empty-like,
and I knocked at its two ends and exhausted it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Am I a man who knows things? No, I know nothing. But when some simple fellow comes to me with a question, his head quite empty, I tap the matter at both ends, and I hold back nothing.”
sentences.n: 知 zhī here is 'knowledge, knowing'. 鄙夫 'a common, rustic fellow' (夫 fū 'a man'). 空空如也 'empty-like': 空空 kōng kōng doubles 'empty' to describe, and 如 'like' (as 7.4 申申如也) makes it 'in an empty way'. Whose emptiness? He Yan's Kong Anguo says plainly the questioner's (其意空空然, 'his mind blank'), and Zhu Xi's 'even to the most foolish' agrees. 叩 kòu 'to knock' (Zhu Xi: 音口, kǒu — a reading modern practice does not keep; we give kòu), here 'to set going, stir up' (Zhu Xi: 發動也). 兩端 'the two ends' — Zhu Xi: like 'both heads': beginning and end, root and branch, high and low, fine and coarse, nothing left out. 竭焉 'used it all up': I hold nothing back. Zhu Xi: Confucius modestly says he has no knowledge, only that in teaching others, even the most foolish, he dares not do less than his utmost. He quotes Master Cheng: the sage's teaching stoops to meet people like this, and still fears they will find it lofty and keep their distance — the sage's Way must come down to them, while a worthy's words must be raised up, or the Way is not honoured; and Yin Tun: the sage's words cover high and low together — close enough that anyone can grasp them, and at their furthest so complete that even a sage could add nothing; this is what 'two ends' means, as in his answer to Fan Chi about humaneness and knowing (12.22). He Yan's own comment on 吾有知乎哉: one who 'knows' does not necessarily tell all he knows; I truly tell all.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
鳳鳥不至，
河不出圖，
吾已矣夫！」
sentences.i: The Master said: “No phoenix comes, and no chart rises from the River. I am finished.”
sentences.n: 鳳 fèng, the phoenix. Zhu Xi: it is a spirit bird; it came in stately array in Shun's time (來儀) and sang on Mount Qi in King Wen's. 河圖 'the River Chart' was carried out of the Yellow River on the back of a dragon-horse in Fuxi's time. All these were auspicious signs of sage kings. 已 'to stop' (Zhu Xi: 止也): 吾已矣 'I am finished'; 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 音扶) closes the cry. Zhu Xi quotes a Mr Zhang (張氏): the phoenix arriving and the chart appearing are omens of a bright culture of letters (文明之祥); the omens of Fuxi, Shun and King Wen do not come, so the Master knows that his own work of letters (文章) is at an end. He Yan's Kong Anguo: when a sage receives Heaven's mandate the phoenix comes and the River brings forth the chart; now Heaven sends no such sign, and 吾已矣夫 means 'I shall not see it'; the River Chart is the eight trigrams.

sentences.t:
子見齊衰者，
冕衣裳者與瞽者，
見之，雖少必作；
過之，必趨。

morph.gloss: hemmed (read zī: Zhu Xi 齊音咨)
mourning hemp (read cuī: Zhu Xi 七雷反)

sentences.l:
When the Master saw those in mourning dress,
those in cap and upper and lower robes, and the blind,
seeing them, though (they were) young, he always rose;
passing them, he always quickened his step.
sentences.i: Whenever the Master saw someone in mourning, or in the cap and full robes of office, or a blind man, he would rise to his feet at the sight of them, young though they might be, and when he passed them he would hurry by.
sentences.n: 齊衰 zī cuī (Zhu Xi: 齊音咨，衰七雷反) is mourning dress of coarse hemp with the hem stitched. 冕 is the ceremonial cap; 衣 yī the upper garment and 裳 cháng the lower (Zhu Xi: 衣上服，裳下服) — cap with upper and lower robes is the full dress of men of rank. 瞽 gǔ 'blind' (Zhu Xi: 無目者). 與 yǔ 'and'. 見 jiàn 'to see'. 作 'to rise' (Zhu Xi and Bao Xian: 起也); 趨 qū 'to walk quickly', a mark of respect (Zhu Xi: 疾行也). 少 shào 'young' (Zhu Xi: 少去聲); Zhu Xi records that some say 少 should be 坐, 'even if he was sitting he rose'. He Yan's text reads 雖少者必作 'even if they were young ones, he rose', which ties 少 to the people seen. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: the sage's heart grieves for the bereaved, honours those of rank and pities those not whole in body; his rising and hurrying happened without his meaning them to; and Yin Tun: this is the sage's sincerity, inside and out one. He Yan's Bao Xian: the cap is the dress of grandees; the Master grieved for those in mourning, honoured those in office, and felt for those not whole.

sentences.t:
顔淵喟然歎曰：「
仰之彌髙；
鑚之彌堅；
瞻之在前，
忽焉在後。」

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.i: Yan Yuan heaved a sigh and said: “I raise my eyes to it and it towers ever higher; I drill into it and it grows ever harder; I catch sight of it in front of me, and suddenly it is behind.”
sentences.n: 顔淵 Yan Yuan is Yan Hui 顏回, courtesy name Ziyuan 子淵, the Master's favourite disciple (顔 is the edition's form of 顏). 喟然 kuì rán 'sighing': 喟 (Zhu Xi: 苦位反) is the sound of a sigh, and 然 makes it an adverb. 之 'it' throughout is, Zhu Xi says, the Master's Way. 彌 mí 'ever more'; 髙 is the edition's form of 高; 鑚 zuān (Zhu Xi: 祖官反; the edition's form of 鑽) 'to drill'; 瞻 zhān 'to look toward'; 忽焉 'suddenly'. Zhu Xi: looking up, the higher it is the less it can be reached; boring in, the harder it is the less it can be entered; now in front, now behind, elusive, it can be given no image. Yan Yuan knew deeply that the Master's Way had no limit and no fixed shape, and sighed over it. He Yan's commentary: it cannot be exhausted; it is elusive and cannot be given a form. The speech runs on past Zhu Xi's comment into the next two units, which are left unquoted.

sentences.t:
夫子循循然善誘人，
博我以文，
約我以禮。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
in due order, stage by stage

sentences.l:
The Master, in due order, is good at leading people on:
he broadens me with letters,
he draws me in with the rites.
sentences.i: The Master knows how to draw a person forward, one stage at a time. He opens me out with letters and gathers me in with the rites.
sentences.n: 循循 xún xún 'in due order' (Zhu Xi and He Yan: 次序貌, the look of proceeding in order), made adverbial by 然. 誘 yòu 'to lead on, draw forward' (Zhu Xi: 引進也). 博我以文 'broadens me with letters' and 約我以禮 'draws me in with the rites': 博 and 約 are adjectives used as verbs, 'to make broad', 'to bring to the essential' (約 yuē; cf. 6.25 博學於文，約之以禮, the same pair). Zhu Xi: broadening with letters and drawing in with the rites are the order of teaching; though the Master's Way is lofty and subtle, his teaching of others goes in order. He quotes Mr Hou (侯氏, Hou Zhongliang): 'broadens me with letters' is extending knowledge and investigating things; 'draws me in with the rites' is subduing the self and returning to the rites (12.1). And Master Cheng: this is where Yanzi praised the sage most aptly — the sage teaches by these two things and nothing else.

sentences.t:
欲罷不能。
既竭吾才，
如有所立卓爾。
雖欲從之，
末由也已。
sentences.l:
I want to stop, and cannot.
When I have used up all my abilities,
it is as if there is something standing there, tall.
Though I want to follow it,
there is no way, and that is all.
sentences.i: I want to give up and cannot. When I have put everything I have into it, there seems to be something standing tall before me; and though I long to go after it, I can find no way to get there.
sentences.n: 欲罷不能 'want to stop, cannot': the verbs simply follow one another, with no 'but'. 罷 bà 'to stop, leave off'. 既 'once, when already'. 如有所立卓爾 'as if there is something standing, tall': 卓 zhuó is 'standing tall' (Zhu Xi: 立貌), 爾 makes it descriptive (like 然). 末 mò 'none' (Zhu Xi: 無也); 末由 'no way through, nothing to go by'; 也已 closes the sentence with finality ('and that is all'). He Yan's text has 未由 'not yet a way', which makes the impasse one he has not yet got past. Zhu Xi: this is Yanzi telling how far his learning had reached — he delighted in it deeply and gave it all his strength; what he saw grew ever closer, and yet there was nowhere to put his strength. Zhu Xi quotes Wu (吳氏): the 'standing tall' lies within everyday conduct, not in something dark and silent; Master Cheng: at this stage the work is hardest — it is sheer, and no great effort will do it; and Yang Shi: from 'the desirable is called good' up to 'great' is the accumulation of effort, but 'great and transformed' lies beyond effort — which is why Yanzi fell short by a hair. Master Cheng again: this is why Yanzi truly knew Confucius and learned well from him. Mr Hu (胡氏, Hu Yin) reads the whole sigh as unprompted: having gained something, Yan tells of his early difficulty and his later attainment and gives the credit to the sage; perhaps it came after 'let me make it my business to act on these words' (12.1), in the time when 'for three months he did not depart from humaneness' (6.5). He Yan's Kong Anguo: the Master broadened me with the literary arts and restrained me with the rites, so that I wanted to stop and could not; I have exhausted my abilities, and what he has established stands tall beyond reach — though I have his good leading, I still cannot reach where he stands.

sentences.t:
子疾病，
子路使門人為臣。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master was gravely ill;
Zilu had the disciples act as his retainers.
sentences.i: When the Master was gravely ill, Zilu had the disciples serve him as if they were the household officers of a great man.
sentences.n: 疾病 'ill, and the illness grave' (He Yan's Bao Xian: 疾甚曰病; as 7.34). 子路 Zilu is Zhong You 仲由, personal name You. 使…為臣 'made (them) act as retainers': 臣 here is the household officer of a noble house. 為 wéi 'to act as'. Zhu Xi: by then the Master had left office and had no household officers; Zilu wanted retainers to manage his funeral. His intention was truly to honour the sage, but he did not know how to honour him. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: Confucius had once been a grandee, so Zilu wanted the disciples to perform the rites of his retainers.

sentences.t:
病閒，
曰：「久矣哉，
由之行詐也！
無臣而為有臣，
吾誰欺？
欺天乎？」
sentences.l:
When the illness eased,
he said: “Long indeed it has been, You's practising of deceit!
Having no retainers, and acting as if having retainers —
whom would I deceive?
Deceive Heaven?”
sentences.i: When he was a little better, he said: “How long has You been carrying on this pretence? To act as though I had retainers when I have none — whom would I be fooling? Heaven?”
sentences.n: 病閒 'the illness had a gap': it eased a little (Zhu Xi: 少差也; Kong Anguo: 病小差曰間). Zhu Xi marks 閒 如字, its basic (level-tone) reading; modern practice reads 病間 jiàn, and so do we. 久矣哉，由之行詐也 puts the predicate first for force: 'long — how long! — You's practising of deceit'. 由 yóu is Zilu's personal name, used by the Master in addressing or speaking of him; 行 xíng 'to practise', 詐 zhà 'deceit'. 無臣而為有臣 'having no retainers, yet acting as one having retainers'. 吾誰欺 'I — whom deceive?': in a question the interrogative object 誰 stands before the verb. Zhu Xi: while ill he did not know of it; when he was better he learned of it, and said: that I ought not to have household officers everyone knows — no one can be deceived, so to act as if I had them is simply to deceive Heaven; and for a man to deceive Heaven there is no greater offence. He takes the blame on himself, and so rebukes Zilu all the more deeply. Kong Anguo reads 久矣哉 'Zilu has had this in mind for a long time, not only today'. The speech runs on past Zhu Xi's comment into the next unit, which is left unquoted.

sentences.t:
且予與其死於臣之手也，
無寧死於二三子之手乎！
且予縱不得大𦵏，
予死於道路乎？

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Moreover, rather than die at the hands of retainers,
would it not be better to die at the hands of you, my friends?
Moreover, even if I do not get a grand burial,
would I die on the road?
sentences.i: Besides, I would sooner die with you, my friends, around me than be tended at the end by retainers. And even without a grand funeral, I am hardly going to be abandoned to die on the road.
sentences.n: The print has 𦵏子死, a misprint for 𦵏予死, corrected here. The subject of the last clause is the Master himself, as in 且予縱不得大葬 just before it, and both collation witnesses (Ruan's 1816 text and He Yan's text) read 予死於道路乎. 𦵏 (U+26D4F) is the edition's form of 葬 zàng 'to bury'. 予 yú 'I'. 與其…無寧… 'rather than…, would it not be better…': 與 yǔ, and 無寧 is simply 寧 nìng 'better, rather' (Zhu Xi and Ma Rong: 無寧，寧也). 二三子 'you, my friends', the disciples. 縱 zòng 'even if'. Zhu Xi: 大葬 is burial with the rites due between lord and retainer; to die on the road means to be left unburied; he further explains to Zilu why things need not have gone as he feared. He quotes Fan Zuyu: Master Zeng, about to die, rose to have his mat changed and said, 'I have what is right, and perish — that is all' (a story from the Book of Rites); Zilu wished to honour the Master but did not see that one who has no retainers may not act as if he had them, and so fell into deceit, an offence that reached to deceiving Heaven; the gentleman must be careful even in small words and acts, and the Master rebuked Zilu so deeply as a warning to learners. And Yang Shi: unless knowledge is complete and intention sincere, a man uses his cleverness for himself and does not know how to act without forcing; again and again he falls into deceit and deceiving Heaven without knowing it — was not Zilu such a man? He Yan's Ma Rong: even if I had retainers and died in their hands, I would rather die in the hands of my disciples; and even if I am not buried with the rites of lord and retainer, with you here, need I fear being left by the road?

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
有美玉於斯，
韞匵而藏諸？
求善賈而沽諸？」子曰：「
沽之哉！沽之哉！
我待賈者也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to wrap away, to keep shut

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “There is a beautiful jade here:
shut it in a casket and store it away?
Seek a good price and sell it?” The Master said:
“Sell it, by all means! Sell it, by all means!
I am one who waits for the price.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “Say we had a lovely piece of jade here. Should it be shut in a casket and laid by, or should we look for a good price and part with it?” The Master said: “Part with it — yes, part with it! Only, I sit still and let the price come to me.”
sentences.n: Zigong poses two choices, each closed by 諸, the fused 之乎 'it?': 'wrap and store it?' or 'seek a good price and sell it?'. 有美玉於斯 'there is a fine jade at this (place)'. 韞 is 'to wrap away' (Zhu Xi: 藏也; modern yùn, Zhu Xi 紆粉反, yǔn); 匵 dú is a casket — He Yan's Ma Rong: 匵，匱也, 'store it in a casket'. 賈 is read jià, 'price' (Zhu Xi: 音嫁; the word later written 價); 沽 gū 'to sell' (Zhu Xi: 賣也). The doubled 沽之哉 is an emphatic 'sell it, by all means!', and 我待賈者也 'I am one who waits for the price'. Zhu Xi: since Confucius had the Way but held no office, Zigong set up these two alternatives as a question; Confucius answers that he should certainly sell, but should wait for the price and not go seeking it. He quotes Fan Zuyu: the gentleman never failed to want office, but he also hated to take it other than by the Way; an officer waiting for the proper rites is like jade waiting for its price — Yi Yin ploughing in the fields, Bo Yi and the Taigong living by the sea, would have ended their days there had there been no Tang or King Wen; they would never bend the Way to follow others, hawking the jade to make a sale. He Yan's Bao Xian: 沽之哉 is a phrase of not hawking — 'I sit and wait for the price'. Variant: He Yan's text ends 我待賈者, without the final particle.

sentences.t: 子欲居九夷。
sentences.l: The Master wanted to live among the Nine Yi.
sentences.i: The Master was minded to go and settle among the nine tribes of the east.
sentences.n: A narrative line, no speech. 夷 is the general name for the peoples beyond the eastern borders of the Chinese states. Zhu Xi: the Yi of the east were of nine kinds (He Yan's Ma Rong says the same), and wishing to live among them is the same thought as 'riding a raft out to sea' in 5.6 — the Way not prevailing at home.

sentences.t:
或曰：「
陋，如之何？」子曰：「
君子居之，
何陋之有？」

morph.gloss: what about that? how would it do?
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Someone said: “It is crude — what about that?” The Master said:
“A gentleman dwells there —
what crudeness would there be?”
sentences.i: Someone said: “But they are a rough, mean people. How could you?” The Master said: “Let a gentleman live among them, and where would the roughness be?”
sentences.n: 陋 'mean, crude, narrow' — of the place and its ways. 如之何 'how about it?' asks what is to be done. 何陋之有 is a fronted object: 'what crudeness — is there?', the object moved before 有 and marked by 之, as 何有 'what is there'. 居之 'dwell in it', 之 standing for the land of the Yi. Zhu Xi: where the gentleman dwells, (people) are transformed (化) — so what crudeness could there be? He Yan's Ma Rong says the same: wherever a gentleman lives, all are transformed.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾自衛反魯，
然後樂正，
雅頌各得其所。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “I came back from Wei to Lu,
and only after that was the music set right:
the Ya and the Song each got its place.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “It was not until I had come home from Wei to Lu that the music was put in order, and the Court Songs and the Hymns each found where they belonged.”
sentences.n: 然後 'only after that' ties the setting right of the music to the return. 樂 is read yuè, 'music'; 正 'set straight' is here a state reached ('was set right'). 雅 and 頌 are two sections of the Odes — the court songs (Ya) and the temple hymns (Song) — which were sung to music. 各得其所 'each got its place'. Zhu Xi: in the winter of the eleventh year of Duke Ai of Lu Confucius returned from Wei to Lu. The rites of Zhou were then preserved in Lu, but its Odes and music were somewhat damaged and out of order; Confucius, travelling everywhere, had cross-checked and verified them and knew their account, and late in life, knowing the Way would never prevail, he came home and set them right. He Yan's Zheng Xuan gives the same date, and says the Way had declined and the music fallen into ruin, so on his return Confucius corrected it. Variant: He Yan's text reads 吾自衛反於魯, with 於 'to'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
出則事公卿，
入則事父兄，
喪事不敢不勉，
不為酒困，
何有於我哉？」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Out in the world, to serve the lords and high ministers; at home, to serve my father and elder brothers; never to let up when there is a funeral to see to; never to be undone by wine — which of these can I claim?”
sentences.n: Four short charges, then the question of 7.2: 何有於我哉 'which (of them) is there in me?'. 出 / 入 are 'abroad' and 'at home', as in 1.6. 喪 is read sāng, 'mourning, funeral rites'. 不敢不勉 is a double negative, 'not dare not exert oneself' — 'never fail to do one's utmost'. 為 is read wéi; in 為酒困 it marks the passive: 'be troubled by wine'. Zhu Xi refers back to his explanation in Book 7 (7.2: modesty — 'which of these do I have?'), and adds that here the matters are humbler still and the thought more pressing. He Yan's Ma Rong glosses 困 as 亂 'thrown into disorder'.

sentences.t:
子在川上曰：「
逝者如斯夫！
不舍晝夜。」
sentences.l:
The Master, standing by the river, said:
“What goes by is like this!
Not pausing by day or night.”
sentences.i: Standing on the riverbank, the Master said: “All that goes by is like this water, flowing on and never resting, day after day and night after night.”
sentences.n: 在川上 'being on (the bank of) the river'. 逝者 'what goes, what passes on' — 者 makes the verb a noun. 如斯 'like this', pointing at the water. 夫 is read fú, a final particle of exclamation (Zhu Xi: 音扶). 舍 is shě, 'to let go, to cease' (Zhu Xi: 上聲). Zhu Xi: the transformations of heaven and earth — what goes passes, what comes follows on, without a moment's halt; this is the original condition of the Way's very substance. Yet nothing points to it so plainly and is so easy to see as a river's flowing, so he spoke of it here to show others, wanting learners to examine themselves at every moment, without the least break. He quotes Master Cheng: this is the substance of the Way — heaven moves without ceasing; the sun goes and the moon comes, cold goes and heat comes; water flows without rest, things are born without end; all make one body with the Way, running day and night and never ceasing. So the gentleman takes it as his model, 'strengthening himself without rest'; and again: since the Han no scholar understood this; it shows the sage's mind, 'pure and unceasing', which is heavenly virtue, and the key lies only in being watchful when alone. Zhu Xi adds his own observation: from here to the end of the book, the sayings all urge people on in learning without stopping. He Yan's Bao Xian reads it more plainly: 逝 is 往 'to go' — everything that goes is like the flowing of the river.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾未見好徳如好色者也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “I have not yet seen one
delighting in virtue as he delights in beauty.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Never yet have I met a man who cared for virtue the way men care for a pretty face.”
sentences.n: 好 is read hào, 'to be fond of', both times (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 徳 is the edition's form of 德 'virtue'. The whole of 好徳如好色 is described by 者 'one who': 'one who loves virtue as (he) loves beauty'. 色 is the face's colour and so beauty, especially a woman's (1.7). Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: to love fair beauty and hate a foul smell is sincerity; to love virtue as one loves beauty would be truly loving virtue — yet people are seldom capable of it. Zhu Xi then cites the Shiji: when Confucius was living in Wei, Duke Ling rode in one carriage with his wife, had Confucius follow in the second carriage, and paraded through the market; Confucius was ashamed of it, and so said this. He Yan's commentary: he deplored that men of his time were thin in virtue and thick in their love of beauty, and so spoke. The saying recurs in Book 15, with a sigh before it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
譬如為山，
未成一簣，
止，吾止也；
譬如平地，
雖覆一簣，
進，吾徃也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “It is like making a mound:
not yet complete by one basket —
if it stops, it is I who stop.
It is like level ground:
though one has tipped out only one basket —
if it goes forward, it is I who go on.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Take building a mound: a single basket short of finishing, if I leave off, it is I who have left off. Take flat ground: with only one basket tipped out so far, if I press on, it is I who press on.”
sentences.n: Two figures of one shape: 譬如 'it is like', the picture, then the verdict 吾止也 / 吾徃也 'it is I who stop / I who go on'. 為 is wéi 'to make'. 簣 kuì (Zhu Xi: 求位反) is a basket for carrying earth (土籠); 覆 fù (芳服反) 'to tip out'; 徃 is the edition's form of 往. Zhu Xi quotes the Documents: 'building a mountain nine ren high, the work fails for want of one basket', and thinks the Master's words come from there. The mound wants only one basket: if it stops, it is I myself who stop; on level ground just one basket tipped: if it goes forward, it is I myself who go. If a learner strengthens himself without rest, little piles up into much; if he stops halfway, all his earlier work is thrown away — stopping and going lie with oneself, not with others. He Yan's commentators read 吾 differently, as the Master's verdict on another man: Bao Xian, one who has built much but stops one basket short — I do not commend him for all his earlier work, for his aim was not carried through, so I do not side with him; Ma Rong, one on level ground who has tipped only one basket — I do not slight him for so little, but side with him for wanting to go on.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
語之而不惰者，
其囘也與？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Told something, and not slackening —
that would be Hui, would it not?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The one who never went slack when I spoke to him — that was Hui, surely?”
sentences.n: 語 is read yù, 'to tell (someone something)' (Zhu Xi: 去聲); 之 is the person told. 惰 duò 'to slacken, grow slack' (Zhu Xi: 懈怠也). 其…也與 'surely it is… is it not?'; 與 is the question particle yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲). 囘 is the edition's form of 回, Yan Hui's personal name. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: when Master Yan heard the Master's words, he understood them in his heart and practised them with all his strength, never departing from them 'even in haste or in danger' (4.5) — like all things moistened by timely rain, flowering and growing; what slackness could there be? The other disciples could not match him. He Yan's commentary: Yan Yuan understood, so when told he did not flag; the others did not understand, so there were times when, being told, they flagged. Variant: He Yan's text reads 其回與, without 也.

sentences.t:
子謂顔淵曰：「
惜乎！
吾見其進也，
未見其止也。」

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.i: Of Yan Yuan the Master said: “How sad it is! I watched him go forward and forward, and not once did I see him come to a standstill.”
sentences.n: 子謂 X 曰 is 'the Master said of X'. 惜乎 'what a pity!' — 乎 here exclaims. Two clauses of one shape, 吾見其 A 也 / 未見其 B 也, with 進 'advancing' against 止 'halting', the two words of the mound saying just before (Zhu Xi: see the previous chapter). Zhu Xi: after Master Yan had died, Confucius grieved for him, saying that he was just advancing and had not yet stopped. He Yan's Bao Xian: Confucius says Yan Yuan advanced and gained without halting, and grieves for him deeply.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
苗而不秀者，
有矣夫！
秀而不實者，
有矣夫！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Sprouting but not flowering —
such there are!
Flowering but not bearing grain —
such there are!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Some shoots come up and never come into ear; and some come into ear and never fill with grain.”
sentences.n: Two lines of one shape: A 而不 B 者, 'the ones that A and yet do not B', then 有矣夫 'there are such!', with 夫 read fú, a final exclamation (Zhu Xi: 音扶). 苗 'shoot' and 實 'fruit, grain' serve here as verbs, beside the verb 秀 'to come into ear'. Zhu Xi: grain first growing is called 苗, putting out its flowers 秀, the grain completed 實; learning that never reaches completion is like this, which is why the gentleman prizes urging himself on. He Yan's Kong Anguo: things that are born but do not grow to completion — a figure for men too.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
後生可畏，
焉知來者之不如今也？
四十五十而無聞焉，
斯亦不足畏也已。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Those born later are to be feared:
how can one know that those coming will not match the present?
At forty or fifty, if nothing is heard of them,
then they are not worth fearing, and that is all.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The young are to be reckoned with: who can say that those who come after will not measure up to us today? But if a man reaches forty or fifty and nothing has been heard of him, he is no longer one to be reckoned with.”
sentences.n: 後生 'those born after', the young, against 今 'the present' (Zhu Xi: 'my present day'). 畏 'to fear, to hold in awe'. 焉 is yān 'how?' (Zhu Xi: 於虔反); in 焉知來者之不如今也 the 之 makes 'those to come not equalling the present' one clause, the object of 知. The second 焉, after 無聞, is a final particle. 四十五十 'forty, fifty' (years old). 也已 piles finality on assertion, 'and that is all'; 已 as the edition prints it, read yǐ. Zhu Xi: the young have years ahead of them and strength enough to build up learning and wait — a momentum to be feared; how do we know their future will not match my present? But if they cannot urge themselves on and reach old age with nothing heard of them, they are not to be feared. He said this to warn people to study while there is time; Master Zeng's saying that a man not known for goodness by fifty will never be heard of expresses the same thought. He quotes Yin Tun: young and not making the effort, old and unheard of — that is the end of it; but who knows whether one who advances from youth will not reach the very height? That is what is to be feared. He Yan: 後生 means the young. Variant: He Yan's text reads 後生可畏也 and ends 不足畏也巳矣, adding particles.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
法語之言，
能無從乎？
改之為貴。
巽與之言，
能無説乎？
繹之為貴。
說而不繹，
從而不改，
吾末如之何也已矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Words of correct admonition —
can one fail to follow them?
Changing by them is what is precious.
Words of mild approval —
can one fail to be pleased?
Tracing them out is what is precious.
Pleased but not tracing them out,
following but not changing —
with him I have no way of doing anything, and that is all.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When words are spoken to you straight, how can you not go along with them? But what matters is that you change. When words are put to you gently, how can you not be pleased? But what matters is that you follow out their thread. A man who is pleased and does not follow the thread, who goes along and does not change — for such a man I am at a loss what to do.”
sentences.n: Two pairs of the same shape — a kind of speech, 能無…乎 'can one fail to…?', then 'X-ing it is what is precious' (為 wéi 'to be') — and a closing verdict. 法語 is 'correcting speech' (Zhu Xi: 正言之, 'telling him straight'; he marks no reading for 語, and we give yǔ); 巽 xùn is 'mild, yielding', and 巽與 'mild and approving' (Zhu Xi: 巽言者婉而導之也, 'speaking tactfully to lead him on'). 説 / 說 is yuè 'pleased' both times; the edition prints the first as 説 and the second as 說. 從 cóng 'to comply'. 繹 'to trace the thread' (Zhu Xi: 尋其緒也). 末如之何 'I have no “what about him”': 末 mò 'nothing, no way' (= 無), and 如之何 'what to do about it'. Zhu Xi: correct words men respect and dread, so they must comply, but if they do not change, it is only compliance to one's face; mild words give no offence, so they must be pleased, but if they do not trace them out, they cannot know where the subtle intent lies. He quotes Yang Shi: correct words are like Mencius's talk of practising kingly government, mild words like his talk of the king's fondness for goods and for beauty; if a man is told and does not grasp it, or refuses it, that is still tolerable; if he understands somewhat, there is still hope he will change and trace it out; but complying and pleased and yet not changing or tracing it out, he never will — even the sage can do nothing for him. He Yan: Kong Anguo, when a man errs and is told the correct way, he will always outwardly comply; being able to change is what is precious; Ma Rong, 巽 is 恭 'respectful' — careful, respectful words please every hearer; being able to trace them out and act on them is what is precious.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
主忠信，
毋友不如己者，
過則勿憚改。」

morph.gloss: to hold as chief, take as first principle
to come up to, be equal to

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Take as chief wholeheartedness and good faith.
Do not befriend those not equal to oneself.
Erring, then do not shrink from correcting.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Hold to wholeheartedness and good faith above all. Do not make friends of those who fall short of you. When you go astray, do not shrink from setting it right.”
sentences.n: These are the closing words of 1.8, and the English is the one given there. Zhu Xi: 重出而逸其半 'a repeat, with half of it lost' — the first half of 1.8 (君子不重則不威，學則不固) is missing here. One difference in the edition's text: here it prints the prohibitive 毋 'do not!', where 1.8 has 無 (which Zhu Xi said there stands for 毋); the word is the same. He Yan's text has 無 here as in 1.8, and an unattributed comment: be careful what you take as chief and whom you befriend, and work at correcting your faults — all of these are ways of gaining.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
三軍可奪帥也，
匹夫不可奪志也。」

morph.gloss: a lone commoner, one plain fellow

sentences.l:
The Master said: “From the three armies their commander can be wrested;
from a lone commoner his intent cannot be wrested.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “An army of thousands can be stripped of its general; one ordinary man cannot be stripped of what his heart is set on.”
sentences.n: Two clauses set against each other, each with 可奪 'can be wrested': the thing taken stands after the verb, the one it is taken from before it. 三軍 is a great state's full levy (7.10). 帥 shuài 'commander'. 匹夫 'a single man', a commoner with no following. 志 'intent, what the heart is set on'. Zhu Xi quotes Mr Hou (侯氏, Hou Zhongliang): the courage of the three armies lies in other men, the intent of a common man in himself; so the commander can be seized but the intent cannot — and an intent that could be seized would not deserve the name. He Yan's Kong Anguo: though the three armies are many, if their hearts are not one, their general can be seized and taken; though the common man is slight, if he holds to his intent, it cannot be taken from him.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
衣敝縕袍，
與衣狐貉者立，
而不恥者，
其由也與？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Wearing a worn robe padded with hemp,
standing with those who wear fox and raccoon-dog,
and not ashamed —
that would be You, would it not?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “To stand in a shabby hemp-padded gown beside men in furs of fox and raccoon-dog and feel no shame — who but You could do that?”
sentences.n: 衣 is read yì, 'to wear', both times (Zhu Xi: 去聲). The first 與 is yǔ 'with'; the last is the question particle yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲), in 其…也與 'surely… is it not?', as 9.19. 敝 'worn' (Zhu Xi: 壞也); 縕 is hemp wadding (Zhu Xi: 枲著也; He Yan's Kong Anguo the same; modern yùn, Zhu Xi 紆粉反, yǔn); 袍 a padded robe — the meanest of clothes. 狐貉 hé (胡各反): furs of fox and raccoon-dog, the noblest. 由 is Zilu's personal name. Zhu Xi: Zilu's aim was such that he would not let poverty or riches move his heart, and he could go on toward the Way; so the Master praised him. Variant: He Yan's text reads 其由與, without 也.

sentences.t:
不忮不求，
何用不臧？
sentences.l:
Not harming, not coveting —
how should he not be good?
sentences.i: One who neither wounds nor craves — how could he fail to be good?
sentences.n: The Master runs on, quoting two lines of an Ode, so the unit is left unquoted. 忮 zhì (Zhu Xi: 之豉反) is 'to harm' (害), 求 here 'to covet' (貪), 臧 'good' (善) — He Yan's Ma Rong glosses 忮 and 臧 the same way. 何用 'by what, why' makes a rhetorical question: 'why would he not be good?'. Zhu Xi: one who can neither harm nor covet — how could he do what is not good? These are lines of 雄雉 'The Cock Pheasant', which he places in the airs of Wei (衛風; the received Odes file it under Bei 邶), and Confucius quoted them to praise Zilu. He quotes Mr Lü (呂氏): when poor and rich meet, the strong is sure to harm and the weak sure to covet. Ma Rong calls it an Ode against greed and spite.

sentences.t:
子路終身誦之。子曰：「
是道也，
何足以臧？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu recited them all his life. The Master said:
“This is a way indeed —
but how is it enough to be good?”
sentences.i: Zilu went on reciting those lines for the rest of his life. The Master said: “That is the way to go, yes. But how is it enough to make a man good?”
sentences.n: 誦 sòng 'to recite, to chant'; 終身 'to the end of one's life'; 之 is the two Ode lines. 是道也 'this is a (the) way'; 何足以臧 'how is it enough to be good?', taking up the Ode's own word 臧. Zhu Xi: reciting it all his life meant he was pleased with his own ability and sought no further advance in the Way, so the Master spoke again to warn him. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: being ashamed of poor clothes and poor food is the great sickness of learners, and the loss of the good heart comes from it; Zilu's aim, being as it was, far surpassed other men's, and an ordinary man who could do this could be counted good; but Zilu's worth should not stop there, and to recite it all his life was no way to advance in daily renewal — so the Master stung him forward. He Yan's Ma Rong: there are still finer things than this; how is it enough to count as good?

sentences.t:
子曰：「
歲寒，
然後知松栢之後彫也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “When the year is cold,
only then does one know that pine and cypress wither after the rest.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “It takes the cold of the year's end to show that the pine and the cypress keep their green when all else has faded.”
sentences.n: 歲寒 'the year is cold' is the condition; 然後 'only after that'. In 松栢之後彫 the 之 makes 'pine and cypress wither late' a clause, the object of 知. 栢 is the edition's form of 柏; 彫 diāo 'to wither, to fade'. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: in a well-ordered age the petty man may not differ from the gentleman; only when gain and harm are at stake, or when affairs change, can what the gentleman holds to be seen. And Xie Liangzuo: an officer in hard straits shows his integrity; in a troubled age one recognizes the loyal minister; he wants learners to be complete in virtue. He Yan's commentary is closer to the trees: in a year of great cold all the other trees die, and then one knows that the pine and cypress are only slightly withered; in an ordinary year many trees also survive, so it takes a cold year to tell them apart — a figure for ordinary men, who in an ordered age can keep themselves in order as the gentleman does; only in a muddied age does one know the gentleman's uprightness, which will not stoop to please.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
知者不惑，
仁者不憂，
勇者不懼。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “The man who knows is never at a loss, the humane man has no cares, and the brave man has nothing he dreads.”
sentences.n: Three lines of one shape, X 者不 Y, 'the one who is X does not Y'. 知 is read zhì, 'wise' (later written 智). Zhu Xi: clarity enough to light up the pattern of things, so not led astray; the pattern enough to overcome selfishness, so not worried; spirit (氣) enough to match the Way and what is right, so not afraid — and this is the order of learning. He Yan: Bao Xian, not perplexed and confused; Kong Anguo, without cares or troubles. The three sayings return in Book 14, with humaneness first.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
可與共學，
未可與適道；
可與適道，
未可與立；
可與立，
未可與權。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “There are men you can study alongside who cannot yet set out with you toward the Way; men who can set out with you toward the Way who cannot yet take a firm stand with you; and men who can take a firm stand with you who cannot yet weigh up the balance of things with you.”
sentences.n: A chain of three steps: each line takes up the end of the one before. 與 is yǔ 'with (him)', the object left out; 共 is gòng 'together'; 適 is shì 'to go to' (He Yan: 適，之也). 權 quán is the weight of a steelyard, and so 'to weigh'. Zhu Xi: 可與 means one can do this thing together with him. He quotes Master Cheng: to study together is to know how to seek it; to go to the Way, to know where one is going; to stand firm, to be firm in aim and hold fast without changing; 權, the steelyard weight by which one weighs things and knows light and heavy — to weigh with him is being able to weigh light and heavy so that it accords with what is right. Yang Shi: knowing that learning is for oneself, one can study together; learning enough to understand the good, one can go to the Way; trusting the Way firmly, one can stand; knowing what fits the time, one can weigh. Mr Hong (洪氏): to talk of weighing before one can stand is like a man who cannot stand trying to walk — he will seldom not fall. Master Cheng again: the Han scholars took 權 as 'going against the norm and according with the Way' (反經合道), hence talk of expedients and stratagems — all wrong; 權 is simply the norm (經). Zhu Xi adds: earlier scholars wrongly joined this chapter with the following 偏其反而 as one, hence that theory, and Master Cheng was right to reject it; yet, reasoning from Mencius's drowning sister-in-law pulled out by the hand, 權 and the norm must still be told apart. He Yan's commentary: some who study take up strange doctrines and do not reach the Way; some who reach the Way cannot establish themselves; some who stand cannot weigh the utmost degree of light and heavy. His commentary reads 唐棣 (9.30) together with this saying — see there.

sentences.t:
唐棣之華，
偏其反而。
豈不爾思？
室是遠而。
sentences.l:
The flowers of the tang-di tree —
how they sway and turn over!
How should I not think of you?
It is that your house is far.
sentences.i: Bush-cherry blossom, tossing and tumbling in the wind. It is not that I do not long for you — only your home is so far away.
sentences.n: Four lines of verse, with no speaker. 棣 is dì (Zhu Xi: 大計反); 唐棣 is the bush cherry (郁李). 華 is read huā 'flower'. 偏 piān: Zhu Xi notes that the Jin shu writes 翩 'to flutter', so 反 should likewise be 翻 'to turn over' — the flowers tossing in the wind. 而 at the line ends is a filler particle (Zhu Xi: 語助). 豈不爾思 fronts the pronoun object in a negative: 'how not you think-of' — 'how should I not think of you?'; 室是遠而 'the house — it is far'. Zhu Xi: this is a lost Ode (逸詩), and of the six modes of the Odes it is an evocation (興): the first two lines have no meaning of their own but only raise the next two; and who 爾 'you' is, is also unknown. He Yan's commentary also calls it a lost Ode, takes 唐棣 as the 栘, and reads it with the 權 saying before it: the flowers first turn away and then come together, and the poem is quoted to say that the way of weighing goes against (the norm) and then arrives at great accord; one who longs for someone and cannot see him blames the distance of his house, as one who thinks of weighing and cannot grasp it blames the distance of its Way. Zhu Xi names that joining as the source of the 'against the norm' theory (9.29).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
未之思也，
夫何遠之有？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “It is that he did not think of it;
now, what distance is there?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The truth is he has not really thought about it. If he had, how could there be any distance?”
sentences.n: 未之思也 puts the pronoun object before the verb in a negative, as 未之有也 (1.2): 'not-yet it think-of'. 夫 is read fú, an opening particle, 'now' (Zhu Xi: 音扶). 何遠之有 'what distance is there?', the fronted object marked by 之, as 何陋之有 (9.13). Zhu Xi: the Master borrows the poem's words and turns them round — the same thought as 仁遠乎哉 'is humaneness far?' in the previous book (7.29). He quotes Master Cheng: the sage never speaks of ease so as to make men's aims proud, nor of difficulty so as to block their advance; he only says 'he has not thought of it; what distance is there?' — words very rich in what they hold back, their meaning deep and far-reaching. He Yan's commentary keeps to its reading of 權: one who thinks should think of the turning back; not thinking is why it seems far; one who can think of it — what distance is there? Weighing can be known; people only do not think of it, and thinking has its order. Variant: He Yan's text ends 何遠之有哉, adding an exclamation. The book closes here.
